title: Purposeful Annotation: A "Close Reading" Strategy that Makes Sense to Students
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This article introduces Stuart's approach to purposeful annotation — a practical alternative to the over-complicated and often poorly-taught concept of 'close reading' — that explicitly links what students mark in a text to what they will do with the text after reading. Stuart traces his own evolution from using 'close reading' as a vague buzzword to understanding it as a cluster of specific, teachable behaviors that readers perform when grappling with complex texts. The central principle of purposeful annotation is that the purpose for reading should determine the nature of the annotations: if the post-reading task is a written response, students annotate their emerging responses and paraphrases of difficult passages. Stuart teaches annotation in stages — modeling the 'annotating as you read' habit with a teacher think-aloud, then providing guided practice, then releasing students to practice independently with the purpose always visible. The article frames purposeful annotation as a tool for developing self-directed, text-savvy readers who can approach any complex assigned text with a clear strategy and a productive mindset.
points: 'Close reading' became a buzzword that obscured specific teachable behaviors — purposeful annotation names those behaviors explicitly and links them to a clear post-reading purpose
The big idea: what students annotate while reading should be determined by what they will do with the text after reading — purpose drives annotation, not the reverse
Two fundamental annotations serve all purposes: responses to the text (reactions, questions, connections) and paraphrases of particularly difficult passages
Purposeful annotation is taught in stages — teacher think-aloud modeling, guided practice with feedback, then independent practice — with the purpose always displayed
When annotation is done well, looking back at margins after reading makes the post-reading task (writing, discussion, debate) dramatically easier — that ease is the proof that it worked
